READING

**Dead mileage**

The three-mile differential is each way, so each of the 22 vehicles on the 44/44A network incurs six extra miles daily. At 313 operating days and £0.63/mile that is:

22 × 6 × 313 × £0.63 = **£26,029/year**

This is the partial figure; school and private-hire vehicles also operate from the depot but no equivalent data is supplied, so the £26,029 is a floor, not a ceiling, on extra running cost.

**Financial comparison over ten years**

| Item | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Rent advantage (KESTERWICK) | (£214k − £118k) × 10 | +£960,000 |
| Dead mileage penalty (44/44A only) | £26,029 × 10 | −£260,290 |
| Capex | Hardstanding / fuel / workshop | −£480,000 |
| Faskally deposit | Non-refundable | −£40,000 |
| **Net undiscounted position** | | **+£179,710** |

The payback on the combined £520,000 outlay against the £69,971/year net annual saving is 7.4 years. Applying a 5% discount rate and the ten-year annuity factor of 7.72, the NPV advantage of KESTERWICK is approximately £20,000. That is a real but modest figure; financial arithmetic alone does not create a decisive case.

**Planning timeline against key dates**

The application was validated 2026-08-14. Adding each scenario's weeks to that date, then a further 22 weeks of construction:

| Scenario | Consent date | Completion date | Hallowbrand end | Nethercote needed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 wk (target) | ~2026-11-13 | ~2027-04-16 | 2027-11-30 | No |
| 34 wk (median) | ~2027-04-09 | ~2027-09-10 | 2027-11-30 | No |
| 61 wk (worst) | ~2027-10-15 | ~2028-03-18 | 2027-11-30 | Yes, ~3.5 months |

The worst-case Nethercote exposure is roughly 3.5 months at £18,500/month = **£64,750**. Even absorbing that, the net ten-year position for KESTERWICK remains positive (£179,710 − £64,750 = ~£115,000). The deposit holds the site to 2028-06-30, which clears the worst-case completion date of ~2028-03-18 comfortably.

The 13-week target almost certainly does not describe typical experience: the median is 34 weeks and the worst case 61. It would be imprudent to plan for anything faster than the median.

**The consent-versus-Hallowbrand-deadline problem**

The Faskally deposit must be paid by 2026-12-05 to preserve the option; the landlord wants a Hallowbrand answer by 2026-12-19. Even in the target scenario, consent arrives ~2026-11-13 — theoretically before either deadline. In the median scenario it does not arrive until April 2027, well after both. In practice, the board would have to let the Hallowbrand offer lapse in December 2026 without knowing whether planning will be granted. That is the sharpest risk in KESTERWICK.

**Cash position**

£640,000 cash plus £200,000 undrawn facility gives £840,000 headroom. KESTERWICK's total draw is £520,000 (deposit + capex), leaving £320,000 of cash and the facility entirely untouched even before trading receipts. This is not a binding constraint.

**The 44/44A bid — the critical factor**

The bid goes in 2027-09-14 for a contract starting 2028-04-01. Depot cost is a fixed line. The contract, covering 22 of 31 vehicles on 313 days a year, is clearly the business's primary revenue.

Under ARDENSHAW the fixed line is **£214,000**.
Under KESTERWICK the fixed line is **£118,000**.

That £96,000/year difference flows directly into the submitted price. Even if Culverstone is not yet occupied on 2027-09-14 — a real possibility under anything beyond the median — the contract period does not start until 2028-04-01. In the worst-case scenario Culverstone is operational by ~2028-03-18, so the depot cost that governs the contract period is legitimately £118,000/year regardless of exactly when consent arrives. KESTERWICK allows Trentmoor to bid at a materially lower cost across the entire next contract term.

Tendered local bus contracts are competed on price. A £96,000/year structural cost advantage is large relative to margins typical in the sector. Losing the 44/44A renewal — the livelihood of 22 vehicles and the anchor of the business — because a competitor can undercut a depot cost that was preventably high would be the worst outcome of all. ARDENSHAW forecloses the ability to compete at the lower number.

**Planning refusal risk**

This is the strongest argument against KESTERWICK. If consent is refused, the Faskally deposit is gone (£40,000), the Hallowbrand offer has lapsed, and Trentmoor must either secure Nethercote long-term at £222,000/year without a workshop (worse than ARDENSHAW in both cost and operations) or return cap-in-hand to the Hallowbrand landlord, who now has all the leverage. That scenario is genuinely bad. Nothing in the problem establishes the probability of refusal, but for a straightforward commercial bus depot — hardstanding, fuel island, two-bay workshop — on a site held by a property estate presumably in appropriate use class, consent is more likely than not. The Verrancombe authority has a record of processing this class of application at every timescale from 13 to 61 weeks, implying they are granting them rather than routinely refusing.

**Nethercote as an operating depot**

No workshop means heavy maintenance must be contracted out at premium rates and turnaround times. With 31 vehicles, that is a real operational risk beyond the headline £18,500/month rent. It reinforces the case for getting to Culverstone rather than extending any period at Nethercote.

**Balance of the argument**

ARDENSHAW offers one thing KESTERWICK cannot: certainty. Rent is known, workshop is available from signature, and the bid number is fixed to the penny. That certainty has real value. But its cost is a structural £96,000/year price handicap going into the most commercially significant decision the business will face in the next two years — the 44/44A renewal. The ten-year financial case for KESTERWICK is positive even on pessimistic planning assumptions, the cash position can absorb it without strain, and the option structure holds the site clear through even the slowest determination Verrancombe has recorded. The planning refusal risk is the one scenario that could make KESTERWICK the wrong choice, and it deserves to be managed: the board should monitor the application closely and, if there are early indicators of a problematic determination, open a quiet conversation with the Hallowbrand landlord before December 19 while the offer is still live.

CALL
  KESTERWICK

GROUNDS
  The depot cost enters the September 2027 contract bid as a fixed line, and KESTERWICK's £118,000 annual rent against ARDENSHAW's £214,000 gives Trentmoor a £96,000/year structural cost advantage in competing for the 44/44A renewal — the contract that runs 22 of its 31 vehicles — which outweighs the planning risk when set against a cash position able to absorb the full capex without drawing on the facility.
